newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Singapore, Malaysia war of words flares anew.
newsitem.headline: Singapore, Malaysia war of words flares anew.

text.p: An intermittent war of words between Malaysia and Singapore has flared up again, this time over criticism of a Malaysian state by Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew.
In a court affidavit filed in a Singapore court on January 27, Lee described Malaysia's Johor state, just across a causeway from Singapore, as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
Johor's Chief Minister Abdul Ghani Othman was quoted in Malaysian newspapers on Wednesday as countering that Malaysia is a democratic country with "freedom of speech".
Lee's affidavit was filed in one of several libel lawsuits brought against Singapore opposition politician Tang Liang Hong after elections in January.

In election campaigning, government officials had accused Tang, a prominent lawyer and advocate of Chinese culture, of being a "Chinese chauvinist" who threatened Singapore's racial harmony. Tang called them "liars", prompting the lawsuits.
Tang fled to Johor soon after the polls, which the governing People's Action Party comfortably won, saying he had received death threats.
In his affidavit, quoted in Wednesday's pro-government Singapore Straits Times, Lee said Johor was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
"It did not make any sense for a person who claims to be fearful for his life to go to a place like Johor," he said.
Johor's Abdul Ghani was reported in The Star daily as saying: "As far as we are concerned, we live in a democratic country where all races live in harmony and there is freedom of speech."

Malaysia and Singapore engaged in acrimonious exchanges last year when Lee raised the possibility of eventual reunification with Malaysia. But he said Kuala Lumpur must first end a policy of special rights for indigenous races and pursue meritocracy.
Malaysia has long accorded preferential treatment to indigenous Malays in areas ranging from business to education.
The programme aims to help Malays, the bulk of the population, catch up economically with ethnic Chinese, who dominate the economy.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad had said that Singapore was using his country as a "bogeyman" to scare voters ahead of the January polls.
Singapore broke away from the Malaysian Federation in 1965 in a policy disagreement.
